paragraphs.text:
A Discourse of the Archbishop of Alexandria on the Palms, and [?]

1. Today we the faithful are celebrating a royal visit, so let us go out to meet the King in a manner worthy of God. It is time, then: let us not sleep. Let us lift our minds up to God; let us not quench the Spirit; let us light our lamps brightly; let us change the tunic of the soul; let us carry the palms like victors; with the crowd let us cry out [?]; with the children, like children, let us sing: "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." For see, he has come; see, he has appeared; see, the King is here. Again he enters Jerusalem; again a cross is made ready; again Adam's bond of debt is torn up; again paradise is opened; again a thief is brought in to dwell there. Again the Church dances. Again the wicked synagogue is widowed; again the demons are put to shame; again the Jews rage; again the faithful are saved. Again all things share in the feast; all things sing the praise of the Master. The heavens rejoice; the mountains exult. You rivers, clap your hands. Come near and cry aloud, as you see

[Note] 1 "Of the feast": the Oxford codex reads "in the feast."

our words become realities. You hills [?], leap; you crowds, shout aloud; you infants, sing hymns; disciples, proclaim; priests, speak out; theologians, give glory; you who are in Zion, go out to meet him; nations, gather together; things in heaven, things on earth, things under the earth, every rank and every age. For he comes to do good to all; he has appeared to have mercy on all, granting joy to all. Being God, he became man, and was seen on earth and lived among men. The Master is with the servants; the one who pays the debt is with the debtors; salvation is with the prodigals; the redeemer is with the condemned; hope is with the despairing; the resurrection is with those who lie below; the merciful one is with the ungrateful; the liberator is with the runaways; the one who owes no account is with those who must give account. The sinless one is with sinners; [?] the ungrateful is he who gives freely and ungrudgingly to all.

2. Do you see, beloved, the mystery of the feast? Do you see the wonders of this day? Yesterday Bethany kept festival; today the whole Church has enjoyed the divine presence. Yesterday he granted life to another; today he himself goes to his death. Yesterday the man four days dead rose up; today he who is to be three days in the tomb arrives. He raised Lazarus on the fourth day to give advance assurance of the common resurrection of our nature, which is composed of four elements. But there Martha is distracted, and she stands as a type of the worship of the Law; here Mary sits at the Master's feet, sketching the Church's love for him and its constant attendance upon him. And he who six days before the Passover, through the five senses of the body, gave back the four-days-dead Lazarus, the one brother, to the two sisters, gave orders for his bonds to be loosed; but now he himself comes to be bound. And he comes, not causing fear or uproar, not surrounded by powers, principalities and authorities as his invisible bodyguard; not seated on a high and lofty throne; not veiled by wings, by fiery wheels full of eyes; not hushing all [?] with trumpets, powers and portents; but hidden in human nature. For this is a coming of love for mankind, not of authority; of forgiveness, not of righteous judgment; of condescension, not of punishment. He appears not in the glory of the Father but in the lowliness of his mother. This coming the wonderful Zechariah foretold to us long ago, and calling creation to gladness he cried out to Jerusalem, as if to the Church in person, saying, "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion." Gabriel too used this same word to the Virgin, saying, "Rejoice,"

and the Savior, risen from the dead, cried to the women, "Rejoice," so that you may learn that it was because of the word of long ago that Eve heard, "In sorrow you shall bear children," that he cried out to the women, "Rejoice," just as Zechariah also proclaimed, saying, "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem." What is the proclamation? Tell us openly, O prophet. "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice." Saying what to Zion? "Behold, your king comes to you, meek." How? You have told of his coming; tell us also the manner of it. On chariots and carriages? With an army and camps and all the rest of the pomp of kings? "No," he says. How then? "Mounted on a donkey and a young colt." What are you saying? Does a king ever arrive sitting on a cheap and lowly colt? "Yes," he says. For he does not come with the same arrogance as others. How then? In the form of a servant; meek as a bridegroom, gentle as a lamb, quiet as a drop falling on a fleece, like a sheep led to the slaughter, like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed: so he comes, wearing mankind's nature, grown brutish, and seated on a brute beast, teaching men not to be proud; bringing down the mighty from their thrones and lifting up the lowly; filling the hungry with good things and sending the rich away empty; bringing with him twelve men, and pitiable ones at that, as his followers, and through them calling the nations together. This is the branch that sprang from the root of Jesse, whom today the children of the Hebrews go out to meet, waving olive branches to him as to one who is merciful, and acclaiming him with palms as the conqueror of death, saying, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." For what does the evangelist say?

3. "And it came to pass that when Jesus drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mountain called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples, saying, 'Go into the village opposite, and as you enter it you will find a donkey and a young colt on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it to me. And if anyone says anything to you, you shall say, "The Lord has need of it."'" Then they put the word of the Word into action: they brought the donkey and the colt, put their garments on them, and Jesus sat on it. Now the village opposite is a type of the present life; for it was opposite, and not near to God. When, then, he drew near to this village, when God became incarnate and was with us, then at last he sends

Variant readings. 1 "Does [a king ever] arrive [sitting on a cheap colt]": the Oxford codex reads "arrives and is held in dishonor, sitting."

the two disciples, that is, the two Testaments. [?]: "Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name." One says, "Awake, O north wind"; the other cries, "Come, O south wind." And David summons the proclamation in the most comprehensive way, and the one that most clearly reveals the cross: from the east and the west, from the north and the sea. Jeremiah sings, pointing out to the nations, as if with a finger, the one who is coming, and saying, "This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge, and afterward he was seen on earth and lived among men." One says to Jerusalem, "Be glad and rejoice, daughter of Zion"; another bids the children, "Praise the Lord, you children." The children answer, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." The psalmist, hearing them, cries to the Master, "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise." The Master bids the people, "Let the children

come to me." The children did well to follow the words of Elizabeth. For when she had said to the Virgin and Mother of God, "Blessed is the fruit of your womb," they say to the one born of her, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." What does "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" mean? He who comes: from where? From heaven, or from the Virgin? He who comes, and goes forward: to where? To his Passion. "In the name of the Lord": that is, of the Father, as Christ himself also said, "I came forth from the Father, and I am going to my Father."

5. Do you see a theological doctrine coming from children who cannot yet speak? The children recognized the Master of creation [by nature itself], while their fathers showed themselves ungrateful. These sang to him as God, and those crucified him as an enemy. These sing, "Hosanna"; those shout, "Crucify him." Young and untaught years grow wise, and those who claim to be wise have become fools and are darkened. The children spread their own garments beneath him, and their fathers divided his garments among themselves. These strip off their own tunics, foretelling the stripping bare of the synagogue, and at the same time showing that we too must put off the old man and submit to Christ; [those cast lots for his tunic]. The children welcome Christ with palms; the fathers come against him with swords and clubs. These bless; those blaspheme. These, like lambs, received the Shepherd; those, like wolves, slaughtered the Lamb. What a strange and unnatural sight it must have been: infants at the breast, nursing in their mothers' arms, holding their own mother's breast with one hand, and with the other waving palm branches to God born of a virgin mother; pouring from their mouths both their mothers' milk and the Master's doctrine; and before they could form words, offering to God the Word the fruit of their lips and saying, "Hosanna," that is, "Save now, in the highest."

6. Who taught you, children? Who [?] you? Who initiated you into the mystery of the Word before the time of speech? Let the ungrateful Jew come forward; let him stand before me, [?] the synagogue. Tell me, Jew: did not all the prophets proclaim to us that Christ was coming? "Yes," he says, "but what is in dispute is this: has he come,

or not yet?" "Not yet," he says. Very well. Let us look, then, at the dignity of the one who is coming, and then we shall know whether he has come or not yet. Do you say that the one who is coming is God, or a mere man? "A mere man," he says. Like David, or David himself? "Like David." You sophist of wickedness! You who are without understanding in your heart! How then does David himself call the one who is coming "Lord" from the Lord, as you heard just now when your own children sang, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has appeared to us"? And again: "The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.'" And again: "The Lord has become king over the nations"; and, "Say among the nations, 'The Lord has become king.'" And who is this king? Hear Isaiah crying out about you: "And they will wish that they had been burned with fire." Why, O prophet? "For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come." What do you say, Jew? See, the prophets clearly foretold that the one who is coming is God.

7. The heretic seizes on the word; the Manichee quickly leaps in and says, "Look, now that you have clearly confessed as God the one who became incarnate of the Virgin, how can you not confess that God suffered and was crucified, if indeed you say that the one who was born and the one who was buried and suffered are one and the same?" O foolish men, slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Listen, be persuaded, and be ashamed. The [?] Word of the Father, united to the earthly substance of his mother, and wishing to renew the image long buried by sin, became man. He kept the loftiness of the Godhead in the lowliness of humanity; he did not change the impassibility of the Godhead into passibility; he did not take on sin from the nature that had sinned, lest what is salvation for us should become dishonor for him, and our exaltation should prove to be his downfall. He did not suffer in his Godhead, however much Mani and Arius and Marcion may rage; otherwise, what need was there for the incarnation? Nor was he crucified as a mere body, however much Paul of Samosata may rail, wanting us to believe in it as the blood of a man. For Scripture says, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree," and "everyone who places his hope in a mere man." A man

could not save us; otherwise Moses, or one of the prophets, would have died for us. But all were under sin. That is why we needed God, the sinless one, made flesh and accepting death for us in the flesh. For this reason the one without flesh takes flesh, so that what is impossible for him through his Godhead he might have as possible through his humanity.

8. He suffers, and he does not suffer. The first, do not reckon to the Word; the second, do not suppose of the flesh of the Word. [Yet do not separate the flesh from the Word.] For I do not separate; I distinguish what is proper to each substance. I say that the Word remained with the flesh, but did not suffer with it; that he hung with it, but did not receive the nails into his own nature; that he was buried with it, but did not die with it; that he was enclosed with it, but was not circumscribed with it; that the soul was separated from the body, but that the Word withdrew from neither of them. Hence Hades was despoiled, when the God-bearing soul went down there; for he went and preached even to the spirits in Hades. And in the tomb the holy body did not see corruption. For the Word was inseparable from his own flesh at every moment, never leaving it bare or abandoned, or without God, or like one of our ordinary bodies. Yet even though our rational nature was united to the Word according to hypostasis, it was not made equal to him. For how could what is recent be made equal to what is before the ages? Or how could what has a beginning be made like what has none? That is why you see him on a colt today, but as a man; for he was twofold. For he grew, and nursed at the breast, and wept, and was in agony, by the law of our nature. For God the Word, when he became flesh, did not refuse the blameless passions of our nature; otherwise he would have refused that nature itself before them. It is not God the Word who sleeps in the boat, for "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep"; rather, it is our flesh that sleeps, which the Word of God put on. The divine nature does not hunger or grow weary from the journey, as Isaiah says: "The great and mighty God shall not hunger or grow weary." How then does he hunger? In the flesh he took from us. How does he suffer? In the flesh he took from us. How does he weep? In the flesh he took from us. How was he put to death? In the flesh; but he is made alive in the spirit. How does he shake [?] the earth? By the Godhead that is from the Father. How does he trample Hades? By the Godhead, which is not from us. How does he say, "I and the Father are one"? By the birth on high before the ages. How does he say, "The Father is greater than I"? By the birth here below from the Virgin. How does he say, "He who has seen me has seen the Father"? By the uncreated nature of the Word. How does he say, "I can do nothing of myself"?

What then? Is the Word powerless compared with [?] the Father? Away with the Arian madness! What is it that says, "Glorify me, Father"? The body of the Word. Who is it that says, "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me"? The Word in the body. How does he say, "My Father and your Father"? He is Father, not of the flesh, but of God the Word who is from him. "My God and your God"? He is God, not of the Word—for how could he be the God of the one who is his equal?—but God of the form of the servant in the Word. "Before Abraham came to be, I am"? It is God the Word in the flesh. "The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you'"? This refers to the recent incarnation of the Word. For it was not one who was begotten of the Father before the morning star and another who was made flesh of his mother in Bethlehem. For even if Paul of Samosata thinks [?] this, Paul of Tarsus does not teach it. But when he signifies the form of God in the form of the servant, he cries, "Who, being the radiance of his glory"; and when, again, he signifies the distinctness of the flesh united in the Word, he says, "And God raised the Lord"; so that, by showing the distinction between the two forms in the one body, Paul the apostle might overthrow both Mani, the [?] of phantoms, and Paul, the worshiper of a man.

9. And you, what do you say? What law do you lay down, you new Manichee, pure champion of his madness? Do you not allow the flesh to be called a nature? "There you are afraid with fear where there is no fear." Have you no respect even for the Master, who said at the time of his Passion, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak"? If it is willing, how is it weak? What form of Christ? What flesh is weak? Surely that of Adam, who became weak. And how is it that he kneels down and prays? Does the Word pray? And how, being God, does he ask anything of God? If, then, he is equal to the Father, as indeed he is equal, he does not pray in his Godhead but as a man. "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again": how does he who has authority need someone else's help? He who says, "Destroy this temple"—that is, his own flesh—"and in three days I will raise it up": how, you enemy of God, is he who raises his own temple destroyed along with the temple? For if he himself was destroyed, does he not surely need [?] someone to raise him? You are afraid, as you suppose, that if you hear that what suffered was not the body of God, you will be worshiping and communing with a mere creature;

but what I dread is this: that I might say the Godhead suffered and died, and so dishonor the whole mystery of the Trinity. For if the Word suffered, while the Father is of an impassible nature, then the substance of the Word was certainly one thing and that of God the Father another. And then why fight the Arians over this? But if there is one substance of the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, and the Word of God suffered in the flesh, then the Father and the Holy Spirit are certainly of a passible and mortal substance too. For if the Word suffered together with the flesh, he certainly also died together with it. And if he died with it, how did he despoil Hades? How did he raise the dead? Moreover, having died, he would certainly be found separated from the living Father. And if so, then at the time of the Passion there was no longer a Trinity in heaven but a dyad, waiting for the Word to rise from the Father's side and ascend into heaven. What lawless audacity! What serpent whispered to these enemies of God and deceived them into declaring the impassible one passible? They make the Creator weaker than his creatures. Are you not ashamed, heretic, at the sun shining on a tree, when the tree is cut down but the sun is neither separated nor cut down along with it, while you say that the Sun of righteousness became passible in his own body? Have you never seen, you evildoer, a murderer or criminal deprived of his head or his hands, while his immortal soul does not die along with his body? So these have received a mortal blow from the Word, and the enemy of God has fallen. But again the enemy of Christ has caught his breath; again the Jew is shameless. Saying what?

10. "See," he says, "it was not God but a man that we killed." To him it is right to say at once: "Be silent! Be muzzled! Put a gag on your mouth!" Granted, you set aside the Law; granted, you killed the prophets. But do you not even blush at David, who says of Christ, "From the womb, before the morning star, he begot me"? The Father above. And again: "The Lord said to me, 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you.'" The one and only Christ has two births: one from the Father, outside time, and the other from his mother, without seed. So when he says, "I gave my back to the whips and my cheeks to blows," these he took from Mary, who was of Judah; and what he took from Judah he gave to the Jews to strike and to scourge. But what he possesses by nature as God, "no man shall see and live." But the Jew says, "How then does the prophet say of the Crucified One,

'And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty'?" But you see again, you ungrateful man, that it is written of him, "He is fairer in beauty than the sons of men." And if you say, "What God can be recent?" I will say to you in turn, "Of what man does the name endure before the sun, and before the moon, for generation upon generation?" And: "He shall come down like rain upon a fleece, and like the drop that falls upon the earth." Again, perhaps you will say, "What God is sold for thirty pieces of silver?" And I will say to you, "What man's blood redeemed and sanctified the whole world?" And if you stumble at this, that you see him sitting on a colt today, why do you not also say what the children, you untaught man, learned without being taught and cried out at the same time: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord"? And that the one sitting on the colt as a man is Lord and God, let your David—though he is not yours—come forward as my witness, who speaks of your children and of the one they praised. Let him tell who it is that is proclaimed as God, standing as it were right in front of the colt and crying out thus: "You who sit on the throne above and on the colt below: O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is exalted above the heavens. Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger," that is, the devil. You who are on the colt as a man are true God: "And we shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers." You who are on the colt established the moon and the stars. You made man a little lower than the angels, and having put on man, you exalted him above every principality and authority, and crowned him with glory and honor. You who are seen on the colt: "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever." And: "A scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom." You loved righteousness and alone hated lawlessness. "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you," because you took the form of a servant. He anointed you, not with the anointing of oil, but with the Holy Spirit; for he is the oil of gladness. That is also why [?] said

…the Virgin who gave birth [says]: “My spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior,” when the Holy Spirit overshadowed her. But consider with me, faithful hearer, how the all-holy Virgin called her Son God. She says: “My God,” according to his divine essence; “My Son,” according to the essence he took to himself from me. “For I did not bear for the world a mere man, but God incarnate. And a trustworthy witness to this is the seal of my virginity. Do not dishonor, O man, the garment that God took from me, lest you insult the one who is clothed in it. Do not insult the tent, for truly it was stitched together without hands for the one who dwelt in it. Do not divide the light from my fleshly lamp, lest you wickedly quench the sun that shone upon the world, who became man without a man. For I knew no man, though I knew God becoming man within me.” 11. You have, O most faithful and most holy flock of Christ, the praises of the feast: leap for joy. You have the divine and spotless teachings of the Church: delight in them. You have the spiritual weapons: fight against the wolves that prey on the flock. Train them not to blaspheme; teach them to contend for the truth; show that the field of our Church, which is Christ's, is clean of all tares. If you are like some Lazarus, bound by the chains of sins or of contrary doctrines, hear today the Word calling to you: “Come out, be loosed, and rise.” And if you are a disciple, fit for teaching, be sent: loose and bring to Christ the colt and the colts, the many who are tied up in error and who stand opposed in the faith and village over against you. And if some object and try wickedly to hinder the loosing of those who are fettered, saying, “Why are you loosing the colt?”—just as they rebuked the blind men to keep them from crying out—then you too say: “The Lord has need of them.” For the Lord sets the fettered free; the Lord gives wisdom to the blind, as you heard today in the Gospel. For since they recognized that the Sun of righteousness had come among them, they rightly cried out to him: “Have mercy on us, Lord, Son of David.” O strange and paradoxical wonders! The blind see again, and the Jews who see are blind. The former confess him as Lord, while the latter ask, “Who is this?” For the evangelist says: “The crowds that went before him and that followed cried out, ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’ And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, saying, ‘Who is this?’” Do you see the strange mystery of the king? Seated on a colt he shakes the city, and nailed to a cross he shakes the whole world, so that you may learn that he has come to shake and destroy the polytheistic error of idols.

12. But observe with me how unfathomable is the mystery of his dispensation. When he shook the prison there below, as the powers above cried out to the powers below, “Lift up your gates, O rulers, that he may enter who says, ‘I am the door,’” the opposing powers, astonished, called back, “Who is this King of glory?” In the earthly Jerusalem, amazed, they ask, “Who is this?” And as he ascended into the Jerusalem above, the spiritual powers, seeing him with a body—they who had never seen him so, because he was bodiless—marveled at the strange manner of his ascent and were at a loss among themselves, saying, “Who is this who comes embodied into the bodiless places?” It is worth marveling how the royal powers ask, “Who is this who comes?”—they who at his birth below cried out and sang together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.” From them the children of the Hebrews, speaking of God, learned well today to say: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest.” For so Luke has recorded it. And in Zion one could see heaven and earth, as it were, answering and greeting one another. Those above say, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace”; those below reply, “Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.” The angels said, “On earth peace”; men cried out, “Peace in heaven.” Why? Because he had come who cries to all, “Peace be with you”—he for whom the prophet prayed, saying, “O Lord our God, give us peace,” that is, “Send your only-begotten Son, so that through him you may be reconciled to us, seeing our nature united to you through him.” Seeing this peace, the choirs above cried, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace”—that is, God's perfect reconciliation with his enemies. The children learned this too and cried, “Hosanna! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.” For what were once enemies have now become brothers, heaven and earth offering one theology and one worship to Christ, who is both heavenly and earthly. Hence those above bid those below to offer their theology: “Let all the families of the nations worship him”; and those below answer those above: “Let all the angels of God worship him.” David cries out to both: “Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad.” The children answered: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” 13. With them let us also sing hymns and keep the feast today—not with worldly pomp, but in a godly way; holding palms not only in our hands but also in our souls. And having made our souls whiter than snow, let us strip from them all the deadness of the old garment of skin, casting away all pride and arrogance. For this is why the King of the bodiless powers comes not on chariots and with armies, but

comes seated on a poor little colt, teaching you not to be exalted upon horses and mules, which have no understanding. Therefore let us too join in singing hymns [?]; with the children let us give glory; with the crowd let us raise the crowd's cry; with Bethany let us leap for joy; with Lazarus let us rise from dead works; with those in Zion let us dance; with the blind who received their sight let us cry out; with infants and old men let us give praise; with the disciples let us proclaim. Let us spread olive branches well along the road of life through almsgiving; like the children, let us cut down the bulk of our over-abundant possessions, and through almsgiving spread ourselves on the road that says, “I am the way,” so that through it we too may find mercy from it, and go with it into the Jerusalem above. Let us enter together into the great temple, both those who go before and those who follow: those who go before are the ones of the third hour, and those who follow are the ones of about the eleventh; those who go before by their deeds, and those who follow by their intention. All of us, with Christ, following together, and having followed, reigning together with him and enjoying the eternal good things, let us send up glory and majesty to him, together with the Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen. [Note a: “Christ”: read “the Christ.”]

[?] OF THE MOST BLESSED EULOGIUS, POPE OF ALEXANDRIA: SEVEN CHAPTERS ON THE TWO NATURES OF OUR LORD AND GOD AND SAVIOR JESUS CHRIST. 1. If after the union our Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature, tell me, which one? That of the one who assumed,

or that of what was assumed? And what has become of the other? If both exist, how is he one, unless one composite was produced from both? And if so, how is Christ not of a different essence from the Father, who is not composite? 2. If our Lord Jesus Christ has never been confessed to be of two natures, how is it possible to say that Christ is of one nature after the union, or even to speak of a union at all? But if Christ has been confessed to have been of two natures, tell me when Christ was of two natures, and when he came to be of one? 3. Is God the Word consubstantial with the flesh [?] assumed by him, or of a different essence? If consubstantial, how has the Trinity not become a quaternity? But if the flesh of God the Word is of a different essence, how is Christ not of two natures? 4. Some speak of “one incarnate nature of God the Word”; and I think you too speak this way. But if this is to be understood as one essence of God and of the flesh, how can the created be identical with the uncreated, and the eternal with what is subject to time? But if it means one nature having another, or held by another, who will tolerate calling one and one not two, but one? 5. If God the Word and the Father are one nature, how are God the Word, the Father, and the flesh not one nature? 6. If God the Word and the flesh are two in no respect, how are God the Word and the flesh not one in every respect? And if God the Word and the flesh are one in every respect, how will the Word not be flesh, and the flesh Word, coeternal with the Father and consubstantial with him as God the Word is? But if God the Word and the flesh are not one in every respect, how are God the Word and the flesh not two in some respect? 7. If it is impossible for God the Word and the flesh to be more united than God the Word and the Father are united, how are God the Word and the flesh united in no respect

Another discourse of Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, on the Trinity and on the divine dispensation of God the Word, one of the Trinity. In the beginning, before the ages, God was; God was before the ages, and God [the Word] was before all things—before the world, before the angels, before heaven, before the sun,

before light, before the stars, before the winds, before the waters, before breath, before the earth, before all creation, visible and invisible. This God, then, who is without beginning and before the ages, the uncreated, by his own will and good pleasure, as he alone knows, and when he knows, and whence he knows, created all the heavenly powers of the angels and of the bodiless hosts and orders—invisible, many-eyed, eyeless [?], six-winged, thrones, heavens. Then after these he fashions the visible world of heaven and earth, to which man also belongs, an image of creation both visible and [invisible], having flesh that is visible and a soul that is invisible. Once this man had been formed, God admonished him, giving him a written law through Moses to turn him back from the error of idolatry. But the law was not able to call man back. Then he sent prophets to admonish, to threaten, and to work wonders. But not even so did erring man turn back from his error. Finally, taking pity on his own creature, God himself appeared on earth, and God the Word lived among men as a man; the form of the Master came down to earth so that the form of the servant might go up into heaven. Then the wicked enemy of mankind, robbed of his former deceit and hope, when he saw himself defeated and crushed through Christ, trampled through the cross, and drowned through baptism, the idols overthrown, idolatry henceforth [?] abolished from among men, and the knowledge of God proclaimed in the world—what does the scheming villain do? He sowed throughout the world a second, different idolatry and error: the tares of heresies. At once, in the time of the apostles, he raised up Simon Magus, the first foul ringleader of the world's heresies, who claimed to be a god. Then, second, Nicolaus, from whom the Nicolaitans took their name. Then Theudas. Then others in succession, his own workers and inventors of error, because of whom very many and various holy synods were assembled by the catholic Church. Thus, at one time, there arose the foul ringleader Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who said that the Son and Word of God is a creature, of a different essence from the Father. Against him the holy and victorious synod of the 318 holy Fathers [?] at Nicaea was assembled, which defined the Son as consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity, and the same as consubstantial with us men according to his humanity, proclaiming him not a creature but the Creator, not a thing made but the Maker of all things. Then later appeared Macedonius, the deceitful bishop of Constantinople, who said that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Because of him the holy synod of the 150 holy Fathers took place, which declared the Holy Spirit consubstantial and uncreated—that is, one essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; one Godhead, one authority, one power, in three hypostases.

Then, about fifty-one years later, Nestorius came forward, the foul and impure prelate of Constantinople, calling the holy Virgin “bearer of a man” and not Theotokos. Because of him the first synod at Ephesus, of the two hundred holy Fathers, took place, which proclaimed the holy Virgin properly and truly Theotokos, and subjected Nestorius to eternal anathema. Altogether about twenty-five years later, Eutyches—an unfortunate man despite his name—archimandrite of the monasteries of Constantinople, emerged, denying that the body of Christ is consubstantial with ours. Then Dioscorus, at that time pope of Alexandria, also came forward, saying that there is one nature in Christ. Because of these two foul heresiarchs the holy synod of the orthodox holy [Fathers] [?] at Chalcedon was assembled. It anathematized these heresiarchs together with Nestorius, proclaimed Christ consubstantial with us according to his humanity, and defined two undivided natures, known in one person. For Christ is one and not two, and his hypostasis is composite. When that heresy too had been extinguished—that is, when the pair of heresiarchs had been anathematized—about a hundred years passed, and the blessed fifth synod took place under the emperor Justinian against Origen, Didymus, and Evagrius, the vain-minded men who babbled that our souls exist in heaven before our bodies and that eternal punishment comes to an end. All of these teachings it rejected, and it anathematized them along with their authors [?]. From the Defenses of Eulogius of Alexandria, against those who say: “If you say that Christ has two essences, then the whole Holy Trinity has become incarnate.” These are the arguments our opponents put forward. For perhaps they think that the essence of the Godhead is divisible, and that one part of it is seen in the Father, another in the Son, and another in the Holy Spirit, as though each hypostasis were known only in part, and not in all the properties of the Godhead. But we have not gone so far in impiety as to think that there is division and cutting in the divine essence. Rather, we say

that each distinct hypostasis possesses without deficiency the marks of the Godhead—creative power and all that belongs to the uncreated nature. For this is how we call the Trinity consubstantial: the same essence is known wholly and completely in three persons. The Father perfectly possesses the essence of the Godhead; so likewise does the Son; so likewise does the Holy Spirit. Paul, the herald of truth, supports this when he says: “For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily.” For he does not say that the Father became incarnate, but that the whole Godhead exists without deficiency in the hypostases—in the Father, in the Son, in the Holy Spirit—existing perfectly in each hypostasis, according to the Savior's words: “All that the Father has is mine.” That is, whatever marks belong to the Father's essence belong also to God the Word, even when incarnate; not as though the Father were the Son, or the Son the Father. For these are names that signify their relation to one another. How then shall we not say that the essence of the Godhead is in Christ without deficiency, when you have confessed [?] that he is perfect God? And how shall we not join those who confess him perfect man in confessing that the whole essence of humanity exists in him? For he did not assume a part of it—flesh without a rational soul, as Apollinarius says—but the whole essence, which is flesh animated by a soul both rational and

For this, existing perfectly and in common in individual human beings, may rightly be called essence. For individuals differ from one another not in essence but in the properties that accompany it—size, color, and, in short, the qualities that characterize persons. And how will they say that Christ is from two natures, unless they understand the term “nature” as meaning essences? For they will not dare to take it as meaning characterized hypostases, since then they would be compelled to say “from two persons” as well; for a characterized hypostasis leads one to think of a person. I say “characterized” so that they may not, by the usual deceit of heretics, posit a hypostasis without its characteristic marks; for then it carries the meaning of essence. And how do they hold that Christ, after the union, is consubstantial with the Father and consubstantial with us? Are they not ashamed to confess two consubstantialities while denying the two [essences]? A counter-argument against those who say that there is a particular essence of the Father, a particular one of the Son, and likewise of the Holy Spirit. If the Word is a nature insofar as he is Word, and not insofar as he is God; and the Father is a nature insofar as he is Father, and not insofar as he is God; and the Holy Spirit is a nature insofar as he proceeds, and not insofar as he is God—then none of them will be God by nature, since “God” is not fatherhood, sonship, and procession; and if not God, then certainly a creature. And again: in the respects in which the Word is distinguished from the Father, in those respects he is also a nature,

and in those same respects the Word is identified with the flesh. In that case he will be of the same nature as the flesh, but of a different nature from the Father. The individual, which has what is common to the nature together with the properties that set it apart from what is common, is not the common nature according to the properties that set it apart from the others of the same essence, but according to the whole nature, which by definition exists wholly in it. For according to the God-bearing Fathers a hypostasis is nothing other than essence with properties: the hypostasis exceeds the essence itself only by the properties that set it apart from the others of the same species. Hence none of these properties is included in the definition of the essence, but only in the description, since they are adventitious, not essential. This is why Basil says that each of us participates in being both through the common principle of essence and through the properties belonging to him, by which he is this person or that. If we remove in thought the accidental properties and consider the nature of Peter in itself, we define it thus: a rational, mortal animal. And since this same definition is given by us for nature taken simply, the same principle will hold both for nature taken simply and for nature as seen in an individual. Where then is the claim that the nature of the individual cannot be common, even if it is often spoken of in terms of the individual, which confirms one and the same thing [?]? So the nature of the individual is common, but the hypostasis is particular. If they object that the Word did not assume the common nature, we reply that we said he assumed the nature, not the hypostatic properties of each individual; for these are what make Judas, or so-and-so, which is evident in all universals [?]. Therefore, when we say that the union came about from common essences, we are not compelled to bring in along with them all the hypostases that fall under them, as the slanderers babble. If, then, we say that he became man having in himself the nature of the Godhead perfect, without deficiency, and superabundant, what necessity is there that in saying this we must bring the Father and the Spirit down into the incarnation as well? For when Peter was crucified or Paul beheaded, each of them having the common human nature full and complete, how did this harm the others who are classed under the same [nature]? It did not, because we are taught that properties belong not to natures but to hypostases. Gregory, in the second book against Eunomius, speaks thus concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: that through these names we are taught not a difference of natures, but only the properties by which the hypostases are known. From the Defenses of Eulogius of Alexandria. I heard one of them, who thought he was arguing nobly, say that there is no nature without a person, but that a person always accompanies a nature: “If, then, there are two natures, there must also be two persons.” How could anyone not pity those who put forward such arguments, who stumble so plainly? And while pretending to [?] Nestorius

[?]…to fight, yet they use his propositions and, as far as it lies with them, embrace his disease? For if there is no nature without a person, but a person accompanies every nature, and they say that the ineffable union in Christ came about from two natures, then on their view Emmanuel is from two persons. The way is then open for the blasphemers to speak freely of two persons in Christ, which is sheer madness. If someone were to unite Peter and Paul, he would not speak of one hypostasis and one person. Hypostases that are persons admit union by essence and union by relation. They do not admit hypostatic union, and they do not produce one person. Hypostases are united by essence, as in the Holy Trinity, where three hypostases are of one essence. Union by relation is understood in many ways: in sharing a name, in equality of honour, in identity of will, and the like. Judas son of James and Judas Iscariot are united by sharing a name. Peter and John are united by equality of honour and identity of will, for each was an apostle and both wished to spread the preaching of Christ. As I said before, then, two hypostases, that is, persons, when united never produce one hypostasis and one person. So if Emmanuel is from two natures, and on their view nature is person, he will also be from two persons, and these do not admit hypostatic union. In this way, by the reasoning of these corrupt men, the dogma of godless division will find [?]. Cyril, who long ago cried out such things against Nestorius, will be cast out, and their view will in no way benefit the right teaching of the faith. Even if some speak of a union of persons, the truth does not require it, and we will not tolerate it. We will walk the unswerving middle road, anathematizing those who introduce a pair of persons while confessing the reality of the two essences in Christ. But perhaps they have put forward this proposition because they are at a loss and are trying to distort our position. When we speak of two natures hypostatically united, they pretend to be deaf. They scrape the words "hypostatically united" off our confession and use against us a proposition that does not fit our confession, saying: "There is no nature without a person." What, then, does this clever proposition of theirs mean? If they mean that natures cannot be seen other than in persons, anyone with even a little knowledge would agree. Everyone knows that, in general, a nature is seen in particular persons, that is, in characteristic hypostases. The nature of the Godhead is seen in the Father, in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. Likewise the angelic nature is recognized in Michael, in Gabriel and the rest, and the nature of humanity in individual persons. But if they want to establish that each nature has its own person attached to it, then in the case of natures, that is, essences, that are not hypostatically united, this argument too

I consider correct. In the case of natures united by composition and hypostatically, however, it is far from the truth. Different natures sometimes come together in an indivisible union and produce one person and one hypostasis. The four elements, for instance, are different essences, yet they produce one body, perhaps of this piece of wood or that stone, seen in its individuality [?], and that is a hypostasis. Since this example seems somehow to suggest mixture and confusion, we should take the example of a human being, who exists in one hypostasis. In each of us the essence of the soul is different from the essence of the body. Yet in each individual the two essences come together and produce one person, of John, say, or Paul or anyone else, while remaining two. The soul did not become flesh, and the flesh did not become soul. Paul, the herald of the truth, is a witness to this when he speaks of "the inner man and the outer" to signify the difference of the essences. Following in his footsteps, John, bishop of Constantinople and teacher of the whole Church, writes as follows in the discourse entitled On the Obscurity of the Old Testament: "For man is a twofold creature, composed of two essences, one perceptible to the senses and the other intelligible, soul, I mean, and body, and he has kinship both in heaven and on earth. Through the intelligible essence he shares with the powers above, and through the perceptible essence he is joined to things on earth, so that he is an exact bond between the two creations." In the same way, then, the union of the two essences in Christ took place in one hypostasis and one person, although the examples show this only dimly. The dispensation in Christ truly surpasses every union and escapes human comprehension. But they linger again in the same diseases and, as the saying goes, wallow in the mire, for they put forward the same things again in a different form. They say: "There is no essence without a hypostasis. So how can one avoid speaking of two hypostases, if you speak of two essences?" Do you see the ignorance of these clever men? They have foolishly brought the same proposition before us again, merely changing the names. For what difference is there between essence and nature, and what difference between person and hypostasis in its distinguishing character? So the same argument will serve us here too. I would say to them: Do you suppose that you make a human being, who is composed of soul and body and seen in distinguishing properties, into many hypostases and many men? Surely you are not so foolish as not to know that the soul is different in essence from the body, and that the body has a different definition of essence. If, as you say, each essence takes on its own characteristic hypostasis, the union means nothing to me, and the one has become two, as it pleases you and your vain

quibbles. But I am composed of two different essences and am not two men. I have both essences, of soul and of body, and am seen in one hypostasis. So what need is there for someone who confesses two essences in Christ to speak also of two individual hypostases? The divine attributes are his by nature, and the human attributes are his because of the hypostatic union. His own flesh did not subsist in another, but in him, as was said before. It had in common with human essence this: to be flesh animated by a rational soul. But it had its particular character in God the Word alone, that is, to be the flesh of God the Word and of no one else. How, then, could something that never subsisted on its own be another hypostasis? Moreover, they should not be ignorant of this either: the holy Fathers often understood hypostasis in place of essence, as Cyril also does. In the third anathema he says: "If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ after the union." Here hypostasis signifies that which subsists. The God-bearing man, who constantly fought against the blasphemies of Nestorius, would not have spoken of hypostases in the one Christ unless he took them in place of essences. Likewise Saint Athanasius says in the letter to the Africans: "Hypostasis is essence, and it has no other meaning than being itself, which Jeremiah calls existence when he says: 'And they did not hear the sound of existence.' For hypostasis and essence are existence, since it is and it exists." If anyone, then, calls the essences enhypostatic in this sense, that is, existing, we would not deny it either. Hypostasis does not differ from essence in being something. The difference is that essence is something held in common, while hypostasis is particular, when along with the universal it also has something particular. So we do not say that our essence in Christ is enhypostatic in the sense of being a characteristic hypostasis and person on its own. We say it is enhypostatic in that it subsists and is. Sometimes hypostasis signifies subsistence, that is, essence, as has been shown, when it lacks the distinguishing properties that are seen in a person. From the Defences of Eulogius, on the same subject.

Whatever is seen in common and in many, and does not belong to one more and to another less, is called essence. Every individual human being equally has the property of being flesh animated by a rational soul, and this is humanity. In this respect, then, although humanity is the mark of two essences, we call it one essence, since it is seen in common and equally in all human beings. But in the case of the hypostasis of Emmanuel, we do not say that the union of Godhead and humanity produced one essence, because an essence must be seen in many, as has been shown. If, then, they say that the two became one essence, others must surely have shared in such an essence too, equally with Emma-

-nuel, and that is not the case. May today's slanderers not be so mad as that, even though they have become thoroughly hostile to God and enemies of the truth. And after other things: We say that humanity, although composed of unlike things, is of one essence. In saying this we look not to the difference between soul and body, but to what is common, because humanity is seen in common in everything that falls under it. For this is the definition of essence, as Basil taught when he said: "As the common is to the particular, so essence is to hypostasis." On this principle of commonality, then, we say that humanity in human beings is of one essence. Every individual human being, in common and equally, is a rational, mortal animal capable of mind and knowledge, and this is the definition of humanity. But when we consider the things from which a human being is made, naming the soul and examining the body, we would not deny their difference in nature or the properties of the essences, even after the union. If the body and the soul were of the same essence, the same account would apply to both, since they would be consubstantial. The body is corruptible, so the soul too would be destroyed, and the statement that the soul is immortal would be shown false by your senseless, empty babbling. From the Defences of Eulogius. We should know that we call a composite one nature when we can no longer properly apply to it the names of its simple components. For example, a body composed of four elements, of water, as we said, and earth, air and fire, we would not properly call water, earth, air and fire. For this reason we call it one nature of body, since we can no longer properly name it by the names of the simple elements. Again, we say that a house is made of stones and timber, but no one who wants to use words properly would call it timber and stones. Again, we say that a human being is made of soul and body, but we do not properly call him body and soul. This is clear because the definition of the soul or of the body cannot be given of the two together. So we say "from two natures," since the things that came together differ in nature and are not consubstantial with each other, yet we hold that the composite is one nature. Speaking properly, we do not call a human being body or soul, although Scripture often uses the freedom of the Spirit to name the whole from the part, since it is not held under the yoke of slavery to the vanity of dialectic. But in the case of Christ the union is inexpressible and ineffable. No human mind could reach it, and no example will be able to match it, in every respect at least. But we say that he is not only from Godhead and humanity. We also apply to him the names of the simple components, for we call the same one God [?]…

[?]…we cannot properly say. For properly and in truth we call the holy Virgin Theotokos, and properly and in truth the same one is man, who truly died and truly rose. For this reason it is impossible to call him simply one nature. That is why we also say "from two natures," since we know that he is composed of Godhead and humanity and recognize that the things that came together differ in nature. And we speak of two distinguishable natures in him, since we hold that the same one is properly God and man. As Cyril among the saints says in the second letter to Succensus: "being one and the same, this and that." Observe that he did not say "being from this and that" (for that too was [?]…). This and that are certainly two, even if you yourself would not wish it. Again, the same Cyril writes thus to Valerian, bishop of Iconium: "Let us confess, then, that what is from flesh is flesh, and what is from God is God, while the one Christ is both at once, being one Son and one Lord with his own flesh." For Christ to be both, what else can it mean than that Christ is two natures? He did not say here that Christ is from both, but that Christ, being one, is both. From the Defences of Eulogius, against those who say that if two essences, that is, natures, are united, they must have become one nature, since things that are united must become one thing [?]. If they mean to establish that they became one thing in respect of the characteristic hypostasis, they speak rightly and very piously, in harmony with those who defined doctrine at Chalcedon. Those Fathers too declare one hypostasis but two essences. The flesh remained flesh, even though it became the flesh of God the Word, that is, he assumed flesh and united it to himself indivisibly. He did not undergo any change into flesh, for the nature of the Trinity is unchangeable God. As I said, then, the two essences have remained unconfused after the incarnation in Emmanuel, the one Christ, the Son of God. But if they say that the two natures have become one essence, they have deceived themselves without noticing. They are positing confusion or change, as if one nature had been changed into the other or confused with it. Things that are united are kept without change and without confusion in their own quantity, and I will show you this clearly by the example of the three hypostases united indivisibly and without confusion in essence, I mean of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. They did not become one hypostasis because they are united. They are united in essence, yet even when united they are recognized in three hypostases. So too in the dispensation of Christ, two essences exist united indivisibly and without confusion. Let the example serve only to expose their rotten proposition, since the union in Christ is the reverse of the case of the

Trinity. There we speak of one and another Someone, so that we do not confuse the hypostases, but not of one and another Something, since the three are one and the same in Godhead. In Emmanuel, on the other hand, the Godhead is one thing and the humanity another, so that we do not confuse the essences. The timeless is not the same as what exists in time, nor the visible the same as the invisible. But he is not one Someone and another Someone, God forbid! By the union both together were made one person and one characteristic hypostasis. From the Defences of Eulogius. So let them not trouble us, those who will not think anything sound but chatter in vain and try to disturb the right and blameless [faith]. We worship one Christ, the Son of God, who was seen in the flesh by those on earth. Yet we know the difference between the Godhead and the flesh. God the Word is timeless, uncreated, impassible, and whatever else befits the divine majesty. His flesh is one with him through the supreme and hypostatic union, on account of which the divine John also cries out: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us." Yet that flesh exists in time and is created and passible. Let us confess that all these attributes of the flesh became those of God the Word. If the flesh is his own, clearly everything belonging to the flesh will be his too. He makes these things his own, even though his divine nature was not subject to them. Divine Scripture teaches us that after the incarnation all the attributes of his flesh belong to God the Word. It says, "We have seen the Lord," speaking of both together. Whoever has seen the flesh of Christ has beheld him whole, even though the Godhead was by nature invisible. Again it says, "they would not have crucified the Lord of glory," although he did not suffer in his divine nature but in his own flesh. In all these passages, then, we are taught that both what befits God and what is human belonged to God the Word made flesh. But where Scripture says that he hungered and thirsted, or was touched or was seen, I understand that he suffered these things not in the divine nature but in the flesh he assumed, in respect of which he was called man.

Of Eulogius [?] of Alexandria: an interpretation of "Simon son of Jonah, do you love me?" When the Lord asked Peter, "Simon son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?", he who knows all things was not asking in order to learn. He was about to entrust the flock to Peter, and he does this to show how much care he has for the flock. By setting over the flock someone burning with great love for the Master, he shows beyond doubt how great his concern for the sheep is. For the same reason he asks a third time, showing his great care for the rational sheep. At the same time he sets out a kind of ranking among those who are shepherded. He commands Peter first to feed the lambs, then the little sheep, and finally, in the third place, he adds the full-grown sheep. The little sheep were sheep once, but through certain lapses they fell short of virtue and perfection, so he turned them back into little sheep. Those who still need milk and elementary teaching are likened to lambs. Those who have fallen short of perfection through some transgressions are likened to little sheep. Those who have risen to perfection in both faith and deeds are likened to sheep. And notice how he puts the imperfect before the perfect, for the Master's chief aim is the salvation of sinners: "For I came," he says, "not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Of Eulogius of Alexandria, among the saints, on "A pair of turtledoves." There are many animals ranked among the clean, so why did the ancients sacrifice only five: the goat, the ram, the ox, the turtledove and the pigeon? Because the Word wants us to bring our senses, which are the same in number, pure to God. Of Eulogius of Alexandria, among the saints. Through the dogs as well, the parable exposes the rich man's extreme harshness. The dogs pitied the poor man's great misery and did what they could, licking his sore and, as it were, wiping it clean with their tongues. But the rich man

was harsher than even the dogs toward a fellow human being, and the dogs themselves convicted him. That is why the fire pursues him without mercy. Of Eulogius of Alexandria. God accepts even these gifts through the poor, as long as from now on we guard against sinning. It is good to make friends, even by means of money gained through greed, of those who are poor in this world but rich toward God. Then, when we fail and have no life-giving righteous deed, those who received mercy from us will welcome us into their own tents because of the good we did them. But if we are not willing to do good even with the mammon of unrighteousness, that is, of greed, how could anyone believe that we would have shown mercy to the needy if we had money earned by our own labour? If we did not share what belonged to others, what we had gained greedily without labour, how could anyone believe that we would share [?] what seems to be our own and the fruit of our own toil? Of Eulogius [?] of Alexandria. "Were forgiven" refers to baptism, and "were covered" refers to repentance. And "to whom the Lord will not reckon" explains "being covered." For true repentance covers sins, so that God does not reckon them.
